name: Apple cider vinegar
short: Case reports: liver injury after long-term use; possible pancreatitis (supplement containing it); low potassium, osteoporosis (large amounts); tooth erosion; gullet injury (tablets); skin burns.
text: The safety evidence for apple cider vinegar consists mainly of single case reports. Taken by mouth: a 60-year-old man with a long history of vinegar consumption developed liver injury attributed to vinegar, which improved after he stopped; an 84-year-old woman developed acute pancreatitis that the authors considered possibly linked to a recently started weight-loss supplement containing apple cider vinegar; a letter, without an abstract, is titled as a report of low blood potassium (hypokalaemia), raised renin and osteoporosis in a patient ingesting large amounts of cider vinegar; and erosive tooth wear in a 15-year-old girl was attributed to drinking a glass of apple cider vinegar every day to lose weight. An article is titled as a report of oesophageal (gullet) injury from apple cider vinegar tablets; after that adverse event, the authors tested eight tablet products and found considerable variability in pH, acid content and label claims, with doubt over whether apple cider vinegar was an ingredient at all. Applied to the skin: a letter, without an abstract, is titled as a report of a chemical burn from topical apple cider vinegar, and a case report describes a chemical burn in an adolescent who used apple cider vinegar to try to remove moles by following instructions found on the internet. A 2025 meta-analysis of seven controlled trials in people with type 2 diabetes found that apple cider vinegar reduced fasting blood sugar and HbA1c and increased insulin; its abstract does not report adverse events. No interaction data were found in the cited sources.
